planting.note: Set out container-grown plants once nights stay warm; this hammock understory shrub tolerates the dry shade and leaf litter found beneath a closed tropical canopy and needs little fuss once rooted in.

directions: Plant in well-drained limestone or sandy soil beneath taller hammock trees, where it naturally forms a multi-trunked understory tree. The showy pink-and-white spider flowers open in late afternoon and are followed by long, twisted seed pods that split to reveal red-coated seeds relished by birds. Established plants handle salt spray and drought well and need little irrigation or fertilizer. Prune only to remove dead wood, since flowering occurs on new growth along the branch tips.
sources: Institute for Regional Conservation (Natives For Your Neighborhood)

planting.note: Transplant from containers in warm weather; young trees grow slowly in heavy shade beneath the hammock canopy and speed up once they reach more light.

directions: A slow-growing relative of sapodilla native to the rockland hammocks of the Florida Keys and lower peninsula, forming a dense, salt-tolerant tree with leathery dark leaves. Small yellowish flowers give way to small round fruits that are edible when fully softened, though far less sweet and fleshy than cultivated sapodilla. It thrives in limestone soils with minimal supplemental water once established and makes a durable, wind-resistant specimen or hedge in coastal landscapes. Give it full sun to light shade and patience, since growth is notably slower than most hammock trees.
sources: Institute for Regional Conservation (Natives For Your Neighborhood)

subcategory: Florida tropical hammock/coastal strand native shrub

planting.note: Nick or soak the hard seed coat before sowing directly where the sprawling, thorny stems can ramble over dunes or coastal thickets without interference.

directions: This scrambling, heavily thorned legume forms tangled thickets along coastal strand and hammock edges, where its curved spines help it climb over neighboring shrubs toward the light. Clusters of small yellow flowers are followed by prickly seed pods holding the hard, gray, marble-like seeds that give the plant its common name and that beachcombers have long collected and polished. It tolerates salt spray, drought, and poor sandy soil without issue, making it a tough choice for a barrier hedge or wildlife thicket. Site it away from foot traffic given its dense spines, and let it sprawl rather than trying to train it upright.
sources: Institute for Regional Conservation (Natives For Your Neighborhood)

subcategory: Florida tropical hammock/coastal strand native shrub

planting.note: Set container plants in brackish or coastal-strand soil in warm weather; this sprawling shrub roots easily from the arching stems that touch the ground.

directions: Coinvine is a sprawling, salt-tolerant legume shrub found along mangrove edges, coastal hammocks, and brackish shorelines throughout South Florida and the Keys. Its single rounded leaflets and small purplish pea flowers give way to flat, disc-shaped seed pods that float and are dispersed by tides, explaining its wide Caribbean and West African range. It thrives in moist, saline-influenced soils but adapts readily to ordinary garden conditions with regular watering while establishing. Use it as a dune stabilizer or informal coastal hedge where its arching, somewhat untidy habit has room to spread.
sources: Institute for Regional Conservation (Natives For Your Neighborhood)

planting.note: Transplant container-grown saplings into limestone-based hammock soil in warm weather; growth is modest at first but picks up as the canopy opens around it.

directions: Soldierwood is a slender, smooth-barked canopy tree characteristic of South Florida and Keys rockland hammocks, named for the way its peeling, mottled bark resembles a soldier's uniform. Clusters of tiny greenish flowers are followed by small dark fruits that draw hammock birds, and the glossy elliptic leaves provide dense partial shade once mature. It grows well directly in limestone outcrops with minimal irrigation once established, making it a low-maintenance shade or specimen tree for a hammock-style native garden. Give young trees some shelter from wind and full sun until they are a few years old.
sources: Institute for Regional Conservation (Natives For Your Neighborhood)
